GET /coach/program/lessons/:id.body:
Most groups read the passage once, quickly, and then talk about something near it. The reading becomes a ticket to the conversation rather than the conversation itself. This lesson is about slowing that moment down, because **Scripture engagement** is the dimension where a small change in the first ten minutes moves the whole hour.

## Read it aloud, and more than once

Ask one person to read the passage aloud, then ask a second person to read it again in a different translation. The second reading always surfaces something the first one hid: a word that changed, a sentence that suddenly sounds strange. In Nehemiah 8 the people stood for hours while the law was read, and the Levites "gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading." Understanding came from staying with the text, not from moving past it.

- Choose readers before the session, so nobody is surprised.
- Keep Bibles open on the table for the whole hour, not only for the reading.
- Read the passage again before the application questions.

## Point to the verse

When someone answers a question, ask a gentle follow-up: *"Where do you see that in the passage?"* It is not a test. It tells the group that every answer is held against the same page, the leader's answers included. Over a few weeks people start doing it unprompted, and that habit is what the rubric is listening for.

> The passage is the teacher in the room. The leader's job is to keep everyone looking at it.

## When someone misreads it

Sooner or later someone will say something the text does not say. Resist correcting them yourself. Ask the group instead: *"Let's look at verse 6 together. What does it actually say?"* The correction comes from the page and from the group, and the person who misread it is not embarrassed in front of everyone. You keep your role as the one who points, not the one who rules.

## Let the story do its work

On the road to Emmaus, two disciples walked with Jesus and did not recognise him. He did not give them an answer; he opened the Scriptures with them, "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets." Their hearts burned while he explained. A good reading time works the same way: the group discovers rather than receives.

## A short exercise

Before your next session, write down three questions that can only be answered by looking at the passage. Avoid questions that anyone could answer without opening a Bible. Then notice, during the session, how often the group's eyes go back to the page.

### What Coach listens for

The Scripture engagement dimension rises when the passage is read aloud, when answers point back to specific verses, and when the leader sends questions back to the text instead of answering them. It falls when the passage is read once and never returned to. ## Before the session

Read the passage yourself at least twice during the week, once quickly for the shape of it and once slowly with a pencil. Mark the verbs. Mark anything that surprises you. Write down the one sentence you would want a visitor to remember if they only came this once. That sentence is not the answer you will give the group; it is the compass you will use when the conversation drifts. Then look for the places where the passage is hard: a name nobody knows, a custom that needs a word of background, a line that sounds harsh. Decide in advance how much background you will give and keep it short. Two sentences of context are almost always enough; anything longer turns the reading time into a lecture, and the rubric notices that too.

## Choosing translations

A group that reads from three translations hears the passage three times without anyone repeating themselves. Pick translations that differ in approach: one that stays close to the original wording and one that aims for plain modern speech. When they disagree, do not settle it yourself. Ask what each one helps the group see. Most of the time the difference is not a contradiction but a texture, and noticing it slows the group down in exactly the right place. If someone reads from a paraphrase, welcome it; it often says aloud what others were thinking but did not dare to say.

## Silence after the reading

After the passage has been read, wait. Count to ten in your head before you say anything. The silence feels long to the leader and short to everyone else. People are still hearing the last verse. If you rush to the first question, you tell the group that the reading was a formality and the real work starts now. If you wait, someone will usually speak first, and what they say is a better first question than the one you prepared. Write it down and come back to it.

## Observation before interpretation

Ask what the passage says before asking what it means. Who is speaking, to whom, where, and what happens next? These questions feel too simple, and that is their strength: everyone can answer them, including the person who has never opened a Bible before. A group that has looked carefully at what is on the page argues less about what it means, because they are arguing about the same thing. Only after the group has described the passage together should you move to what it meant for its first readers, and only after that to what it asks of us this week.

## Keeping the passage in view

During the discussion the passage tends to fade, and the conversation slides toward opinions and stories. Your job is to bring it back, lightly and often. Read a single verse again when the group seems stuck. Ask someone to find the word that answers the question. Put the key verse on a card in the middle of the table. None of these takes more than thirty seconds, and each one tells the group that the text is still the centre of the hour. Leaders who do this well rarely need to say 'let's get back on track'; the passage does it for them.

## When the passage is difficult

Some passages are painful or confusing: violence, judgement, a promise that seems unkept. Do not skip them and do not explain them away too quickly. Name the difficulty plainly: 'This is a hard passage, and it is all right to find it hard.' Then help the group look at it honestly. What is happening in the story? What do we learn about God here, and what do we not learn? Where does the rest of Scripture shed light on it? A group that has been allowed to struggle with a hard text trusts its leader more, not less, and that trust shows up later in the dimensions about honesty and prayer.

## Bringing it home

The last reading of the passage, just before the application questions, is the one people take home. Ask someone different to read it. Then ask a question that connects one verse to one specific moment in the coming week: a meeting, a meal, a conversation they are dreading. Keep it concrete and keep it small. A group that leaves with one verse and one moment in mind has done what the reading was for, and that is what the next lesson, on questions that lead somewhere, builds on.

## Reading with a mixed group

Most groups hold people at very different places: someone who has read the Bible for forty years beside someone who opened one for the first time last month. Reading together is the one moment when they stand on equal ground, because everyone has the same words in front of them. Protect that. Avoid jargon in your introduction, and never assume the group knows where a book sits in the story. A sentence such as 'this letter was written to a small church in a port city' costs ten seconds and keeps the newest person in the conversation. When an experienced member offers a long cross-reference, thank them, then bring the group back to the verse in front of everyone. The aim is not to keep the experts quiet but to keep the passage the common ground.

## Noticing who reads

Keep a quiet note, after each session, of who read aloud. Over a month you will see a pattern: the same three people read every week, and some never do. Some people do not read aloud because they are not confident readers, and that is a reason to ask privately, never to put them on the spot. Others simply have never been asked. Asking someone to read is the smallest form of giving them a part, and it is often the first step toward the leader development the rubric looks for in the Building Ministry cluster. A person who has read the passage aloud owns it a little more than one who only listened.

## What to do with questions you cannot answer

Sooner or later the reading raises a question you cannot answer: a word whose meaning you do not know, a historical detail, a theological puzzle that has occupied scholars for centuries. Say so. 'I don't know; let's find out before next week' is one of the most trustworthy sentences a leader can say, and it models the honesty that the Being Real cluster rewards. Write the question down where the group can see you do it, and bring an answer, or a better question, the following week. That small act of follow-through links one session to the next, which is exactly what the homework references dimension is listening for.

## Reading as worship

Finally, remember that reading Scripture together is not only a teaching technique. For many people in your group it is the closest they come, all week, to hearing God speak. Treat the reading with that weight. Do not rush it to make up for a late start, do not talk over the last verse, and do not apologise for how long it is. A group that learns to listen to the passage with attention learns something about listening to God, and that lesson outlasts every question you prepared. Coach cannot score that directly, but almost every dimension it does score grows out of it.

## A note on time

In a ninety-minute session, the reading and the observation questions together should take about twenty minutes. Less than ten usually means the passage was rushed; more than thirty usually means the leader is doing the talking. Keep an eye on the clock without letting the group see you do it. If the reading runs long because the group is genuinely discovering something, let it run and cut a later question instead. The shape of the hour serves the passage, not the other way round.
